content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Secretariat collected forms from participants and shared a summary of the results with the guideline development group. If unanimous consensus was not achieved during the primary decision-making process, additional time was allocated for further deliberations, followed by a second round of online voting. If unanimity was still not reached, a two-thirds majority vote among the present members of the guideline development group was required to approve the proposed recommendation, as per the secondary decision rule. Divergent opinions were allowed to be documented in the guideline. Voting results were retained by WHO for up to five years. Despite the lack of unanimous consensus, over 80% of the group members supported the recommendation as a strong one. WHO staff and external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading were not permitted to participate in the decision-making process. Two co-chairs with expertise in group management and evidence interpretation were nominated and approved at the start of the consultation. WHO Secretariat members were available throughout the meeting to guide the process but did not vote or hold veto power. Six content experts peer-reviewed the draft guideline, and a public call for comments on the final draft was issued in August 2014. Stakeholders who wished to provide feedback were required to submit a signed declaration of interests form. Feedback from various stakeholders was incorporated, and the finalized guideline was submitted for clearance by WHO before publication. In accordance with WHO’s Basic Documents, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their involvement. Declarations of interest from guideline development group members were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition and issuing invitations. Participants acted in their individual capacities, not as institutional representatives, and verbally declared potential conflicts of interest at the start of each meeting. WHO’s procedures for managing conflicts of interest were strictly followed, as outlined in its guidelines for expert declarations. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil disclosed that her employer, an international non-governmental organization focused on improving micronutrient status among vulnerable populations, was primarily funded by the Canadian government. Her organization, the Micronutrient Initiative (MI), worked on salt iodization efforts, particularly with small-scale salt processors. Dr. De-Regil participated in deliberations related to salt iodization recommendations but recused herself from voting on the guideline. Dr. Maria Elena del Socorro Jefferds, employed by the CDC, declared the CDC’s partnership with the International Council for the Control of Iodine Deficiency Disorders Global Network. She was allowed to fully participate in deliberations and decision-making for the guideline. Dr. Lynette Neufeld disclosed that her employer had received funding in the past four years for salt iodization research and programming, though she was not leading these initiatives. In a prior role with MI, she had commissioned iodine-related research. Dr. Neufeld participated in deliberations but recused herself from voting on salt iodization recommendations. Ms. Rusidah Selamat declared her membership in Malaysia’s National Technical Food Fortification Committee and her publications on iodine deficiency and iodized salt consumption in Malaysia. She was permitted to participate in the guideline development group after declaring her affiliations. All other members verbally declared their interests, which were deemed irrelevant to the guideline on food-grade salt iodization. External experts also declared their interests but did not participate in deliberations or decision-making. The guideline is scheduled for review in 2024. The WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, in collaboration with internal partners, will coordinate the update following formal WHO procedures. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate during the review process.
